title: Field-order and comment tolerance prompt catalog
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight catalog of prompt variants intended for model onboarding verifiction and regression testing focused on two related failure modes: (1) field-order sensitivity (models that break or reorder required keys) and (2) tolerance for non-standard JSON constructs that appear in real world outputs (comments, trailing commas, stray commas, duplicate keys, and extra unexpected fields).

Why this set: 
- During onboarding we often see models that produce perfectly valid text but produce JSON that is brittle: parsers fail on trailing commas, comments, or when the model changes field order and downstream consumers expect a stable order/format.
- This catalog intentionally mixes schema-conforming and non-conforming prompts so we can measure both strict adherence and tolerant parsing robustness.

Test categories (high-level):
1) Field-order stability: verify that required fields appear and are not broken across lines or arbitrarily nested.
2) Non-standard tokens: comments (//, /* */), trailing commas, unquoted keys, single quotes, and commas after arrays.
3) Duplicate keys and precedence: repeated keys with different values — check determinism and preferred resolution strategy.
4) Extra/unknown fields: model introduces fields not in schema (should be allowed but flagged).
5) Type coercion tests: numbers as strings, boolean as "true" string, null vs missing.
6) Minimal/compact formatting vs pretty printed: model should produce a single JSON object parseable in both cases.

Core schema used for examples (reference):
- name: string (required)
- id: integer|string (required)
- version: string (optional)
- features: array of { feature_name: string, enabled: boolean } (optional)
- metadata: object (optional)

Prompt templates (use these to generate eval cases). Each prompt is deliberately short so testers can reuse and remix.

PROMPT 01 — strict-field-order (expectation: exact key set and parseable JSON)
Task: Return a single JSON object exactly matching the schema. Keep keys in the order: name, id, version, features, metadata.
Example instruction to model: "Produce a JSON object for a model descriptor. Keys must appear in this order: name, id, version, features, metadata. Do not include extra text."
Edge variants: request the same but emphasize compact output (no spaces/newlines).

PROMPT 02 — permuted-order (measure reordering)
Task: Same schema, but do not instruct order. Score if model consistently emits same order across 10 runs.
Variant: force random seed or different temperatures and check stability.

PROMPT 03 — comment-injection (tolerance for comments)
Task: Ask the model to output JSON but allow inline comments explaining fields. E.g., "Include a short //comment after the version field explaining the release note."
Objective: We expect models to sometimes include comments. Downstream parser may fail; record presence of comments as a format warning.

PROMPT 04 — trailing-commas-and-single-quotes
Task: Intentionally ask the model for a quick example and include trailing commas in the expected output: "Show the object with human-style trailing commas and single quotes — we will parse leniently."
Objective: Measure rate of trailing commas and single-quote usage.

PROMPT 05 — duplicate-key-resolution
Task: Prompt the model to deliberately return the id field twice with different values. E.g., "Return two id entries: one old_id and one id with current value; both keys should appear."
Objective: Observe which value appears last (common convention) and whether model uses arrays or nested objects to represent duplicates.

PROMPT 06 — unknown-extra-fields
Task: Ask model to add 1–3 additional fields that are plausible but not in schema (company, created_at, tags).
Objective: Track common extra fields and decide whether to allow them or enforce a whitelist.

PROMPT 07 — typed-coercions
Task: Provide values that could be typed differently. Example: id: "42" vs id: 42, enabled: "true" vs true, features: "[]".
Objective: Measure frequency of type as strings vs native types and add heuristics for tolerant parsing or explicit cast rules.

PROMPT 08 — compact-vs-pretty (formatting variability)
Task: Ask for compact single-line JSON then for pretty-printed multi-line JSON. Score whether both are valid and if newline placement breaks downstream ingestion.

PROMPT 09 — newline-in-strings and escaped characters
Task: Include description fields that contain newlines, backslashes, and unicode. E.g., description: "multi-line\nstring with a \\ backslash".
Objective: Ensure model uses proper escaping so the JSON remains valid.

PROMPT 10 — relaxed-json-with-comments-exercise (stress tolerant parsers)
Task: Model can include JS-style comments and trailing commas; we will test a tolerant and strict parser and record failures.

Scoring heuristics (suggested):
- PASS (strict): JSON parses with a strict JSON parser (RFC 8259) and all required fields present and correct types.
- WARN (lenient): Does not parse strictly but parseable with a tolerant parser (json5-like) OR contains mild issues (comments, trailing commas, single quotes) but all semantic fields recovered.
- FAIL: Required fields missing, types incompatible for core fields (e.g., id completely non-numeric when number expected), or gross structural errors.

Regression checklist for onboarding: 
- Baseline run: 10 prompts x 20 seeds (200 samples) across model variant (quantized vs fp16) and temperature settings (0.0, 0.2, 0.8).
- Track: strict pass rate, lenient pass rate, common error classes.
- If strict pass rate < 90% for hosted target we recommend a follow-up: prompt engineering + explicit JSON wrapper or a post-processing parser step.

Evaluator notes and quick heuristics: 
- When encountering duplicate keys, prefer the last-occurring value but flag these as nondeterministic.
- If type coercion is consistent (e.g., id always string), consider adding a conversion step in the SDK rather than forcing model changes immediately.
- For comments and trailing commas: prefer server-side tolerant parsing (json5 mode) for non-critical internal flows, but for external APIs prefer strict outputs and improve prompts.

Example expected outputs (good vs bad):
GOOD (strict):
{"name":"tokenizer","id":42,"version":"v1.2","features":[{"feature_name":"cache","enabled":true}],"metadata":{"notes":"stable"}}

WARN (lenient parsable):
{
  // model metadata
  "name": "tokenizer",
  "id": "42", // id as string
  "version": "v1.2",
  "features": [
    {"feature_name":"cache","enabled": true},
  ], // trailing comma
}

BAD (fail):
{name:"tokenizer", id: "forty-two", features: "should be an array"}  // missing required typed id and bad types

Quick TODOs (follow-ups):
- Add converter tests: run outputs through json5 parser and our strict parser and produce diffs for common fixes.
- Create an automated harness that replays each prompt N times and outputs a CSV with columns: prompt_name, run_id, strict_parse, lenient_parse, errors, normalized_json. (Ticket: JIRA ENG-9876)
- Draft SDK post-processor recommendations: cast id -> int if numeric string; coerce boolean-like strings; sanitize comments and remove trailing commas.

Notes-to-self: This catalog tries to surface the types of oddities we actually see in the first 3 weeks after onboarding new model families (especially community models with looser text generation patterns). Keep it small, iterate quickly, and fold high-frequency patterns into the Optimize recommendations.

Related resources:
- Confluence page with parsing heuristics: confluence:APPLIED-ML/formatting-tests
- Serving-runtime PR that added tolerant-json parsing: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2345
- Jira epic for onboarding regression: JIRA-ENG-9876

Changelog (brief):
- 2024-08-15: initial draft (Aisha).
- 2024-09-02: added duplicate-key and typed-coercion prompts (Diego).
- 2025-01-10: added scoring heuristics and TODOs for harness (Linh).

----
End of catalog. Use these templates to generate coverage for onboarding jobs and include results in the model eval summary.
